article.summary: Atomic Agent is a local-first agent whose durable memory lives outside the chat transcript in a versioned SQLite database. It combines profile facts, searchable notes, links, lessons, and procedures, then injects bounded selected context into prompts. This review describes pinned source and documentation; it does not report a runtime or benchmark result.

who_what.text: The curated roster lists Atomic Agent at the AtomicBot-ai repository locator. The official repository identifies the project as a local-first AI agent, rather than a standalone memory database. The inspected repository pages do not establish an individual maintainer role.

architecture.text: Durable memory is held in a dedicated SQLite database separate from session storage. The schema has profile facts and freeform memory notes; notes carry content, timestamps, source, optional session and working-directory identifiers, tags, recall counters, and lifecycle fields. FTS5 mirrors note content for keyword retrieval, and schema migrations are versioned.

Specialized stores and workers add profile history, links, lessons, procedures, votes, reflection, reconciliation, and consolidation. Profile facts have stable row IDs, valid-from timestamps, supersedes/superseded-by links, pinning and contextual keywords, disable state, vote score, and name-grounding state. Replaced facts remain as history rather than overwriting the previous version.

The context provider builds bounded prompt sections from recalled notes, a compact note index, and separately budgeted lessons and procedures. Optional graph-link expansion appends neighbors after ranked recall while deduplicating IDs; the provider filters already-recalled notes from the index. Memory remains outside the transcript and only selected previews/facts enter a turn.

The user guide says current defaults enable profile, notes, reflection, recall/index injection, and query rewriting; embeddings, typed-note extraction, and segmented reflection are optional and disabled by default. Configuration overrides and migrations can change installed behavior, so source defaults are not a claim about any particular installation.

behavior.text: Reflection can form bounded profile facts and notes from completed-turn observations. A deterministic grounding guard skips probe-only or one-off instruction turns and rejects unsupported user names, assistant identity claims, and instructions recast as enduring preferences. Name-like facts are kept in storage while unchecked, but the prompt renderer omits them until grounding checks find support in user messages.

Notes can be added through the memory store and explicit memory tools, while profile facts use ProfileStore.set. Profile updates create a new row in the supersession chain, preserving earlier values for history. Optional reconciliation marks replaced notes as superseded and the context provider omits them from ordinary recall and the index; archive/consolidation can preserve a note by distilling it into a lesson.

Removal and turning an entry off are distinct lifecycle choices. The schema ties embeddings to note rows with a delete cascade, and ProfileStore keeps historical profile rows when an active fact is removed. The store also supports disabling notes and profile facts: disabled rows remain listed but are excluded from recall, search, prompt context, and consolidation. The user guide cautions that deleting a chat does not delete durable memory.

Keyword recall uses FTS5/BM25. When embeddings are configured, hybrid recall blends normalized BM25 with cosine similarity; notes found only by meaning fill remaining slots above the configured similarity floor and pass the same working-directory and tag filters. Query rewriting is enabled by default and heuristic-gated. If vector recall errors, the notes tool falls back to keyword recall. TUI search and lesson/procedure recall remain keyword-only.

The optional vector path scans up to a configured brute-force ceiling (documented default 2,000 vectors); above it, it checks the newest vectors plus vectors for keyword hits and records overflow. Background backfill embeds one note at a time in small batches. During backfill recall stays keyword-only to avoid ranking a partially indexed corpus as if it were complete.

Note rows preserve source (agent or user), timestamps, optional session ID, working directory, and tags; profile history links a replacement fact to the version it supersedes. These fields provide item-level lineage, but the inspected model does not establish claim-level citations to source passages. The store accepts an optional metrics sink for dedup decisions, eviction sweeps, and clock-skew detections; formation documentation describes per-session tracking of repeated sub-runner failures/timeouts and operator warnings. These are source-visible instrumentation paths, not observed telemetry.

Project scope is represented by a nullable working_dir on notes. The context provider applies a project filter only when a working directory is supplied; without it, retrieval spans projects. The memory recall tool lets its caller/model select scope, and profile facts have no project-scope key. The reviewed source shows filtering behavior, not a principal-based authorization boundary or a tested isolation guarantee.

metrics.evidence: Source defines ranked note retrieval and bounded context, but no answerable or unanswerable probes were run or adjudicated.
Profile versions and note supersession provide source-visible correction mechanisms; their accuracy and stale-value behavior were not measured.
Removal and disable paths exist, but no accepted-delete workflow was exercised and no post-deletion leakage probes were run.
Working-directory filtering is conditional on supplied scope and profile facts lack a scope key; no cross-project or principal isolation probes were run.
Stored notes have source/session metadata, but this review found no measured claim-level support or citation coverage result.
The implementation exposes bounded retrieval paths and an embedding scan ceiling, but no retrieval latency distribution was collected.
No controlled write acknowledgment and scheduled recall probes were performed.
Prompt sections and bounded index/previews are source-visible, but token usage and cost were not measured in this review.
SQLite tables and embeddings are inspectable in source, but persistent bytes attributable to stored items were not measured.

limits.text: This is a bounded inspection of selected documentation and TypeScript source at the verified main head. It does not establish retrieval quality, answer correctness, safe erasure of database pages/backups, cross-principal isolation, runtime latency, storage efficiency, or current configuration on any installation.

Working-directory filters are caller inputs and profile facts do not carry a working-directory key; the reviewed behavior should not be interpreted as an authorization guarantee. The embedding path may scan only a bounded subset when the corpus exceeds its ceiling, and this review did not measure recall impact.

Project documentation reports defaults, but local configuration and migrations can override them. No system, benchmark, or tests were run, and no source-visible metric field has been treated as a measured outcome.

benchmark.note: Benchmark status is not_run. No Atomic Agent runtime or benchmark workload was executed. Metric definitions and fixture counts describe a protocol and planned probes, not measured results.
